Arthur John Arberry: The language moves with a rhythm that is at once complex and completely natural. It has a compelling cadency, a majestic sweep of sound that can strike the ear like a symphony, even when the listener does not fully comprehend the literal lexicon.
Carlo Alfonso Nallino: Arabic possesses a staggering richness of synonyms, but they are not redundancies. Each synonym represents a distinct shade of meaning, a microscopic shift in perspective, making it one of the most analytically precise tongues in existence.
Charles A. Ferguson: Arabic is a classic profile of diglossia, where two varieties of a language exist side by side throughout the community, each having a definite role to play
H. A. R. Gibb: The beauty of the Arabic language is not merely in its vocabulary, but in the cadence of its words. It possesses a strange power of mesmerizing the human mind, where the rhythm and sound often match the grandeur of the thought itself.
Ibn Khaldun: The Arabic language is a habit (malakah) embedded in the tongue, similar to any craft or biological skill. Its purity is maintained not by birth, but by the continuous, rigorous immersion in its unmatched grammatical architecture.
Louis Massignon: It is the Arabic language that has given the analytical tool to Arab thought. It is a language of coordinates, structurally designed to catch the fleeting moments of psychological introspection and spiritual transition with unmatched fluidity.
Philip Hitti: No language has ever succeeded in expressing the finest nuances of thought through a mathematical system of root derivations as effectively as Arabic. Each word is built from a three-letter triconsonantal root, growing logically like branches from a tree trunk.
